This is a good (or at least revelatory) debate insofar as Anthropic has come to uniquely dominate many of the major controversies surrounding AI. There’s little doubt, as @GavinSBaker put it, that Dario and Anthropic did themselves no favors by being so vocal about existential risks and the necessity of centralized, preemptive regulation—almost to the point of sounding messianic about Anthropic’s certain central role in any such eventuality.

I’ve been a long-term fan of Claude (still the model I use most), even if I’ve found it a bit more predictable, verbose, and nagging lately. I respect the good-faith concerns Dario has voiced. But it’s hard to ignore the inherent tension in the position.

If Anthropic is uniquely far ahead, it should be able to “pace the frontier” through its own efforts. If the risk is instead diffuse and subject to a classic prisoners’ dilemma—where one party pausing simply means someone else keeps pushing—then coordinated restraint looks extremely hard to enforce, especially once other countries are factored in. The US and USSR managed limited collaboration on nuclear non-proliferation; I don’t think it’s fair to presume China cares less about AI safety across the same dimensions the rest of us do.

Ultimately the whole discussion can feel self-indulgent to anyone not already deeply inside the industry or “AGI-pilled.” A relatively small group in SV is fully convinced of the accelerating or imminent arrival of systems capable of superintelligence, large-scale displacement, and maximal harm. To most others this still looks like a large stretch.

AI has become far more useful, especially with agents and tool-calling. Yet even the frontier models remain well short of reliable independent task completion. They still show persistent brittleness and goal drift, and they continue to require meaningful human supervision—particularly once you move beyond short-horizon digital tasks into longer-horizon or higher-complexity work.

The stronger existential warnings seem to require imagining systems that are orders of magnitude more capable than anything currently available. Against that backdrop, the gap between “useful and improving” and “existential” remains large enough that the public often hears the stronger claims as overfit storytelling. Demanding concrete demonstrations of the capabilities that would make those claims urgent is not an unreasonable request; it is simply the normal standard of evidence.

I think showing more of such evidence would be far more persuasive and productive at coordinating AI safeguards than further public lecturing about what may be coming.

Bitcoin’s 1+ year HODL Wave is rising again.

This is a metric that shows the percentage of BTC supply that hasn’t moved onchain for at least a year.

Here's how it compares with other timeframes:

→ Last August: ~64%
→ February: ~59%
→ Now: ~61%

A lot of BTC that moved around this time last year has now been sitting still for 12 months, so it gets counted in the 1+ year bucket.

On the other hand, Glassnode shows long-term holders sold a net ~212K BTC over the past 30 days.

So most BTC is still sitting untouched for over a year, even though some long-term holders have started selling recently.

I wouldn’t call 61% an accumulation signal yet.

But we're getting there.

Thus, when measured on a multi-year timeframe, it's actually pretty challenging to get more sustained tax revenue from that approach, once an economy is this financialized.

If you were in San Francisco during the crypto token boom, the AI token boom feels weirdly familiar, especially at the extremes.

Extreme displays of wealth. This constant paranoia that you need to make generational money right now or somehow you’ll end up poor. Everyone around you seems to be getting richer, so even if you’re doing objectively well, you start feeling like you’re the only idiot missing the trade haha

Then come the shady deals, insiders making absurd money, people optimizing every relationship for upside, very little loyalty, and a surprising amount of betrayal the second incentives change.

It creates this strange atmosphere where ambition, FOMO, greed and genuine technological excitement are all mixed together.

The huge difference is that AI is actually an extraordinary underlying technology. The economic value being created is real, the productivity gains are real, and the benefit to humanity is enormous!!

So from my experience, the boom can feel unhealthy at the edges while the thing we’re collectively building is incredibly healthy and important.
